## Motivation

1. Comparison is fundamental to biological discovery. In the sequencing era, our
comparisons are often based on large-scale molecular readouts.

   * In functional genomics, we compare molecular profiles before and after knocking out genes.
   * In cancer biology, we compare molecular profiles in cancer versus healthy tissue.
   * In microbiome studies, we compare microbial species communities before and after treatments.
   * In single cell eQTL studies, we look for cell-type-specific expression profiles that differs across genotypes.

   Viewed more abstractly, this is a problem of comparing the frequency of
   genomic features across conditions, potentially accounting for secondary
   factors, like timepoints or patient characteristics, that can also influence
   the observed frequencies.

   <img src="figures/problem_overview.png" width=500/>

2. The overarching goal of differential expression analysis is to identify
genomic features that vary systematically across conditions of interest. From an
analysis perspective, there are two fundamental challenges:

   - The "usual" statistical assumptions do not immediately apply.
   - There may be thousands of features of potential interest. The more we
   analyze, the greater the risk that irrelevant features appear associated just
   by chance.

   The first problem motivates _normalization methods_, and the second motivates
   _multiple hypothesis testing methods_. There have been many proposals
   for both normalization and multiple hypothesis testing. We will focus on the
   specific procedure adopted by limma, though many of the ideas of this
   approach appear throughout the literature.

## Example

3. Before diving more deeply into the statistics, let's look at a prawctical
code example using the limma
package.
The block below loads our software packages and sets a random number seed for
reproducibility.

   ```{r}
   library(limma)
   library(edgeR)
   library(tidyverse)
   library(airway)
   set.seed(20260923)
   ```

   We'll analyze the
   [airway dataset](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/data/experiment/html/airway.html),
   which comes from an RNA-seq experiment of how gene expression profiles change
   in smooth muscle tissue treated with dexamethasone. The data come from four
   cell lines, and for each line, there are paired treatment and control
   samples.

   ```{r}
   data(airway)
   airway
   ```

4. This experiment object includes counts and context. The `assay` slot includes
the counts of each gene transcript across the measured samples. The `rowData`
and `colData` slots include contextual data about the genes and samples,
respectively.

   <img src="figures/coldata diagram.png" width=400/>

   This object was assembled by the `airway` package, but in
   practice, we would create our own using the `SummarizedExperiment` function,
   whose inputs are the counts matrix and the contextual data about each sample and
   gene. For any regression models that we run below, we will need the relevant
   variables to be defined as column names in the `colData`.

   ```{r}
   head(colData(airway))
   head(rowData(airway))
   assay(airway)[1:4, 1:4]
   ```

   The first line below makes sure that `untrt` is the reference level, so a
   positive $t$-statistic is interpreted as the treatment being larger than the
   control. Limma expects the experiment object to be stored in a `DGEList`
   ("differential gene expression list"), which reorganizes the counts and
   context present in the original experiment object. The `SE2DGEList` function
   converts from `SummarizedExperiment` to `DGEList`.

   ```{r}
   airway$dex <- relevel(airway$dex, ref = "untrt")
   dge <- SE2DGEList(airway)
   ```

5. We next filter genes that are expressed at very low levels. The commands that
follow normalize the data, which we discuss in detail below. The most important
part of this code block is that `model.matrix` specifies the factors that
influence gene expression. Here, both the cell line and the dexamethasone status
are allowed to influence gene expression levels. This is encoded in the
formula object `~ cell + dex`. Both variables were columns in the `colData`
slot of our original experiment.

   ```{r}
   keep <- filterByExpr(dge, group = dge$samples$dex)
   dge <- normLibSizes(dge[keep, ])
   design <- model.matrix(~ cell + dex, data = dge$samples)
   v <- voom(dge, design, save.plot = TRUE)
   ```

6. We use the output from normalization as input for hypothesis testing. The
`topTable` output shows genes that limma declares to be the most significantly
different between dexamethasone and control settings. My point in showing the
code here is that even though the statistical discussion below might seem long,
the actual implementation is only a few lines.

   ```{r}
   fit_raw <- lmFit(v, design)
   fit <- eBayes(fit_raw)
   topTable(fit, coef = "dextrt")
   ```

## Linear Models Background

```{r}
#| label: fig-setup
#| echo: false
#| include: false
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)

ink <- c(
    primary = "#0b0b0b", secondary = "#52514e", muted = "#898781",
    grid = "#e1e0d9", axis = "#c3c2b7"
)
pal_group <- c(A = "#A53C61", B = "#487150")

theme_note <- function(base_size = 12) {
    theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
        theme(
            panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
            panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = ink[["grid"]], linewidth = 0.3),
            axis.text = element_text(colour = ink[["secondary"]]),
            axis.title = element_text(colour = ink[["primary"]]),
            strip.text = element_text(colour = ink[["primary"]], face = "bold"),
            legend.position = "top",
            plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = base_size),
            plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA)
        )
}
theme_set(theme_note())
```

7. The machinery that underlies both normalization and multiple hypothesis
testing is the linear model. We briefly detour to review the mechanics of
hypothesis testing through linear models. There will be math, but the math is
necessary to make our understanding precise.

8. Let $y_n$ represent gene expression levels across samples $n$. Imagine that
data come from two groups (e.g., healthy and disease, or knockout and control)
and that are both Gaussian distributed. The groups may have different means
$\mu$ but are required to have the same variances $\sigma^2$.

   $$
   \begin{align}
    y_{n} \sim
    \begin{cases}
    \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{A}, \sigma^2\right) & \text{for } n \in \text{Group A} \\
    \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{B}, \sigma^2\right) & \text{for } n \in \text{Group B}
    \end{cases}   \end{align}
   $$

   <img src="figures/two-group diagram.png" width=300/>

   If we want to see whether the true (unobserved) group means are the same, we
   can compute,

   $$
   t = \frac{\bar{y}_A - \bar{y}_B}{s\sqrt{1/N_A + 1/N_B}}.
   $$

   This is the differences in observed means of groups A and B, adjusted
   according to an empirical estimate $s^2$ of the within-group
   variance^[Ideally $s^2 \approx \sigma^2$]. This adjustment accounts for the
   spread within each group when interpreting the difference in means.

9. We will say that when the means of the two groups are equal, the null
hypothesis holds. The reason for the naming is that when the two groups have the
same mean, there is no need to further examine subgroup differences (null $\iff$
nothing more to look at). Formally, this is denoted,

   $$H_{0}: \mu_{A} = \mu_{B}$$

   Even when $H_{0}$ holds, the observed difference in sample means will be
   nonzero on any actual dataset, and therefore $t \neq 0$.  In the plot below,
   the normal densities denote the true data distributions in each group, the
   points represent the observed data, and the horizontal lines reflect the
   observed sample means.

   ```{r}
   #| label: lm-setup
   #| echo: false
   #| include: false
   n_per_group <- 5
   sigma <- 1
   n_sims <- 10000
   effect <- 2
   slope <- 1.5
   df_t <- 2 * n_per_group - 2

   simulate_two_groups <- function(n_sims, n_per_group, effect, sigma) {
       expand_grid(sim = seq_len(n_sims), sample = seq_len(2 * n_per_group)) |>
           mutate(
               group = if_else(sample <= n_per_group, "A", "B"),
               mu = if_else(group == "A", effect, 0),
               y = rnorm(n(), mu, sigma)
           )
   }
   t_statistics <- function(sim_data) {
       sim_data |>
           summarise(
               n = n(), mean = mean(y), ss = sum((y - mean(y))^2),
               .by = c(sim, group)
           ) |>
           pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = c(n, mean, ss)) |>
           mutate(
               sigma_hat = sqrt((ss_A + ss_B) / (n_A + n_B - 2)),
               t = (mean_A - mean_B) / (sigma_hat * sqrt(1 / n_A + 1 / n_B))
           )
   }
   group_dotplot <- function(data, subtitle = NULL, population_means = NULL, population_range = NULL) {
       population_layer <- NULL
       if (!is.null(population_means)) {
           population <- expand_grid(
               group = names(population_means),
               y = seq(population_range[1], population_range[2], length.out = 300)
           ) |>
               mutate(
                   center = match(group, c("A", "B")),
                   density_width = 0.36 * dnorm(y, population_means[group], sigma) / dnorm(0, 0, sigma)
               )
           population_layer <- geom_ribbon(
               data = population,
               aes(y = y, xmin = center, xmax = center + density_width, fill = group, group = group),
               orientation = "y", inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.18, colour = NA
           )
       }
       ggplot(data, aes(group, y, colour = group)) +
           population_layer +
           geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
           geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = 0.85, position = position_jitter(width = 0.06, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
           geom_crossbar(
               stat = "summary", fun = mean, fun.min = mean, fun.max = mean,
               width = 0.5, linewidth = 1, middle.linewidth = 1
           ) +
           scale_colour_manual(values = pal_group, guide = "none") +
           scale_fill_manual(values = pal_group, guide = "none") +
           labs(x = "Group", y = "y", subtitle = subtitle)
   }
   null_histogram <- function(subtitle = NULL) {
       ggplot(null_t, aes(t)) +
           geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
               binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0,
               fill = ink[["grid"]], colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2
           ) +
           geom_line(data = t_curve, aes(t, density), colour = ink[["primary"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
           scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-6, 6), breaks = seq(-6, 6, 2)) +
           labs(x = "t-statistic", y = "Density", subtitle = subtitle)
   }

   null_data <- simulate_two_groups(n_sims, n_per_group, effect = 0, sigma = sigma)
   null_t <- t_statistics(null_data)
   one <- filter(null_data, sim == 1)
   t_curve <- tibble(t = seq(-6, 6, length.out = 400), density = dt(t, df_t))

   alt_data <- simulate_two_groups(1, n_per_group, effect = effect, sigma = sigma)
   t_obs <- t_statistics(alt_data)$t
   population_range <- range(one$y, alt_data$y, c(0, effect) - 4 * sigma, c(0, effect) + 4 * sigma)

   n_cov <- 12
   cov_data <- tibble(
       group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = n_cov),
       X = runif(2 * n_cov, 0, 4),
       y = if_else(group == "A", effect, 0) + slope * X + rnorm(2 * n_cov, 0, sigma)
   )
   fit_null <- lm(y ~ X, data = cov_data)
   beta <- coef(lm(y ~ group + X, data = cov_data))
   ```

   ```{r}
   #| label: fig-lm-null-population
   #| echo: false
   #| fig-width: 4.5
   #| fig-height: 4
   #| out-width: 400px
   group_dotplot(
       one,
       subtitle = sprintf("True means: A = 0, B = 0; SD = %s\nObserved t = %.2f", sigma, t_statistics(one)$t),
       population_means = c(A = 0, B = 0), population_range = population_range
   ) + coord_cartesian(ylim = population_range)
   ```

   However, the further the statistic $t$ is from zero (either negative or
   positive), the less plausible the null hypothesis $H_0$ becomes. The example
   below is a case where $H_{0}$ does not hold, and this is reflected in the
   relatively larger $t$-statistic.

   ```{r}
   #| label: fig-lm-alt-population
   #| echo: false
   #| fig-width: 4.5
   #| fig-height: 4
   #| out-width: 400px
   group_dotplot(
       alt_data,
       subtitle = sprintf("True means: A = %s, B = 0; SD = %s\nObserved t = %.2f", effect, sigma, t_obs),
       population_means = c(A = effect, B = 0), population_range = population_range
   ) + coord_cartesian(ylim = population_range)
   ```

10. Under the null hypothesis $H_{0}$, what would be typical values of $t$? We
can answer this with a simulation. I've simulated 5K null datasets,
computed the associated $t$-statistics, and put those statistics into a
histogram. These turn out to follow a clean distribution^[A $t$-distribution with eight degrees of freedom.], and it's in fact
possible to derive a theoretical formula for it, which is overlaid.

    <img src="figures/lm_01_null_distribution_animation.gif" width=600/>

11. This is useful because it tells us that anything that doesn't fall into this
distribution is evidence against the null hypothesis. I generated one
sample where the true group difference is 2 and I've overlaid the $t$-statistic
from that dataset onto the null from before.

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-lm-observed-t
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 8
    #| fig-height: 3.6
    #| out-width: 700px
    tail_region_r <- filter(t_curve, t >= t_obs)
    tail_region_l <- filter(t_curve, t <= -t_obs)
    group_dotplot(alt_data, subtitle = sprintf("True difference = %s", effect)) +
        (null_histogram(subtitle = "Observed t on the null distribution") +
            geom_area(data = tail_region_r, aes(t, density), fill = pal_group[["A"]], alpha = 0.6) +
            geom_vline(xintercept = t_obs, colour = pal_group[["A"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
            geom_area(data = tail_region_l, aes(t, density), fill = pal_group[["A"]], alpha = 0.6) +
            geom_vline(xintercept = -t_obs, colour = pal_group[["A"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
            annotate("text",
                x = t_obs + 0.2, y = 0.3, hjust = 0, colour = ink[["primary"]], size = 3.4,
                label = sprintf("t = %.2f\np-value = %.3f", t_obs, 2 * pt(t_obs, df_t, lower.tail = FALSE))
            )) +
        plot_layout(widths = c(1, 2))
    ```

    This is the essential logic of hypothesis testing: if we see a statistic
    that doesn't fall into the bulk of the null distribution, then we have
    evidence that the null hypothesis is false. A $p$-value is defined as the
    area of the distribution with larger magnitude than the test statistic, and
    it is a measure of the strength of this evidence (smaller area $\to$ less
    likely to come from the null).

12. So if we're willing to believe the Gaussian assumption, we have a procedure
for comparing means across two groups. But in genomics, we often want to analyze
several factors at once, either because we have several treatments to give
simultaneously or because we need to control for secondary factors. For many
centuries, the guiding principle was to analyze one factor at a time, varying
one but fixing all the others. This would mean working with separate subsets of
data.

13. One of the major insights of statistics is that it can be beneficial to
analyze multiple factors at once, because it allows you to share evidence across
all subsets^[Stephen Stigler lists this as #6 in his ["7 Pillars of
Statistical Wisdom"](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674088917).]. The
idea is to proceed like in Figure 4, where we care about the difference between
A and B, but the response is influenced by a secondary factor $x_n$. If we
subsampled into data within a narrow range of $x_n$, then we would be discarding
most of the information.  Conversely, if we ignored this factor and only
compared the $y_n$ values, then the groups would become more blended and we
would struggle to detect a difference.

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-lm-parallel
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 5.5
    #| fig-height: 3.8
    #| out-width: 450px
    lines <- tibble(
        group = c("A", "B"),
        intercept = c(beta[["(Intercept)"]], beta[["(Intercept)"]] + beta[["groupB"]]),
        slope = beta[["X"]]
    )
    x_arrow <- 3.4
    arrow_df <- tibble(
        x = x_arrow,
        y = lines$intercept[2] + lines$slope[2] * x_arrow,
        yend = lines$intercept[1] + lines$slope[1] * x_arrow
    )

    p_parallel <- ggplot(cov_data, aes(X, y, colour = group)) +
        geom_abline(intercept = coef(fit_null)[1], slope = coef(fit_null)[2], colour = ink[["muted"]], linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.5) +
        geom_abline(data = lines, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = group), linewidth = 0.9) +
        geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = 0.85) +
        geom_segment(
            data = arrow_df, aes(x = x, xend = x, y = y, yend = yend), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = ink[["primary"]], linewidth = 0.5,
            arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.06, "in"), type = "closed")
        ) +
        annotate("text",
            x = x_arrow + 0.08, y = mean(c(arrow_df$y, arrow_df$yend)), hjust = 0, size = 3.4,
            colour = ink[["primary"]], label = "group difference"
        ) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = pal_group, name = "Group") +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))) +
        labs(x = "Covariate X", y = "y")
    p_parallel
    ```

14. In this case we might want to test the null hypothesis $H_{0}$ that the
lines for the two groups are exactly overlapping. The main trick is to subtract
out the effects from the $x_n$ and see whether there still remains a difference
between the two groups. That is, after subtracing the $x_n$ effects (i.e.,
looking at the gaps between the points and the dashed line), we return to the
setting above.

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-lm-adjusted
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 8
    #| fig-height: 3.6
    #| out-width: 650px
    adjusted <- mutate(cov_data, y = y - beta[["X"]] * X)
    (p_parallel + theme(legend.position = "none") + labs(subtitle = "y depends on group and X")) +
        (group_dotplot(adjusted, subtitle = "Removing the X effect") + labs(y = expression(y - hat(beta) * X))) +
        plot_layout(widths = c(3, 2))
    ```

    This is exactly what a linear model does. The formula becomes more
    complicated, but we can again derive a $t$-statistic that has a closed form
    null distribution under $H_{0}$.

15. The fact that we can make comparisons between groups while accounting for
the influence of many factors is what makes linear models such a versatile
statistical method. The example here uses a straight line for $x_n$ but the same
machinery works generally, including when the effects are nonlinear, when the
slopes of the lines are not parallel, and when we have a treatment with more
than two levels.

## Normalization

16. Unfortunately the Gaussian assumption doesn't make sense for genomics data.
But the literature has found ways to salvage their applicability.  This is done
is through a process called normalization, and it lies at the heart of limma.

17. There are two issues that stand in the way of making the Gaussian
assumption. The first is that sequencing assays return counts of different
genomic features, and these are not continuous measurements like the Gaussian.
The second is that each sample's mean can depend on its sequencing depth.
Sequencing depth is a technical factor that can obscure the actual biological
differences between conditions.

18. An idea that addresses both problems is the log counts-per-million (CPM)
transformation. Suppose that the expression for gene $g$ in sample $n$ is
$y_{ng}$. Arrange all these data into a samples-by-genes matrix^[This is the transpose of the format used in `SummarizedExperiment`, but it is more common to write in this format in statistics.] $Y \in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times G}$. The logCPM transformation is,

    $$
    y_{ng} \rightsquigarrow \log\left(\frac{y_{ng} + \frac{1}{2}}{\sum_{k}y_{nk} + 1} \times 10^{6}\right)
    $$

    The $\frac{1}{2}$ and $1$ offfsets help us avoid $\log\left(0\right)$, which
    is undefined. Besides this, the fraction inside of the log converts each
    sample into something like a relative frequency of gene $g$ in sample $n$
    (it would be exactly this without the offsets). This removes differences in
    sequencing depths. The $10^6$ is where the "per-million" name comes from.
    Finally, by taking the log transformation, we convert discrete counts into a
    continuous scale where the normal distribution assumption is more
    believable.

19. The three genes in Figure 6 are shown before and after applying the CPM
transformation. The data are described in more detail in the code example below.
For XIST, the Gaussian approximation makes much more sense after the
transformation.

    ```{r}
    #| label: pickrell-setup
    #| echo: false
    #| include: false
    library(tweeDEseqCountData)
    data(pickrell1)
    data(annotEnsembl63)

    pk_counts <- exprs(pickrell1.eset)
    pk_samples <- data.frame(sex = factor(pickrell1.eset$gender, levels = c("male", "female")), row.names = colnames(pk_counts))
    pk_genes <- data.frame(gene_id = rownames(pk_counts), symbol = annotEnsembl63[rownames(pk_counts), "Symbol"], row.names = rownames(pk_counts))
    pk_dge <- DGEList(counts = pk_counts, samples = pk_samples, genes = pk_genes)
    pk_keep <- filterByExpr(pk_dge, group = pk_dge$samples$sex)
    pk_dge <- pk_dge[pk_keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] |> normLibSizes()

    pal_sex <- c(male = "#A53C61", female = "#487150")
    pickrell_genes <- c("GAPDH", "KDM5D", "XIST")

    # reused below for the airway examples as well
    tidy_expr <- function(mat, dge, scale) {
        as.data.frame(mat) |>
            rownames_to_column("gene_id") |>
            pivot_longer(-gene_id, names_to = "sample", values_to = "value") |>
            left_join(dge$genes, by = "gene_id") |>
            left_join(dge$samples |> rownames_to_column("sample"), by = "sample") |>
            mutate(scale = scale)
    }

    # reused below for the airway and YWHAB examples as well
    expression_scales <- function(dge, symbols) {
        keep <- dge$genes$symbol %in% symbols

        list(
            `raw count` = dge$counts[keep, , drop = FALSE],
            `log-CPM` = cpm(dge, log = TRUE)[keep, , drop = FALSE]
        ) |>
            imap(\(mat, scale) tidy_expr(mat, dge, scale)) |>
            list_rbind() |>
            mutate(
                symbol = factor(symbol, levels = symbols),
                scale = factor(scale, levels = c("raw count", "log-CPM"))
            )
    }

    pk_three_genes <- expression_scales(pk_dge, pickrell_genes)
    ```

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-pickrell-normalization
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 8
    #| fig-height: 5
    #| out-width: 700px
    plot_three_genes <- function(data, xlab) {
        ggplot(data, aes(value, fill = sex)) +
            geom_histogram(bins = 25, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2, position = "identity", alpha = 0.7) +
            scale_fill_manual(values = pal_sex, name = "Sex") +
            facet_wrap(~symbol, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
            scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
            labs(x = xlab, y = "Samples")
    }
    (
        plot_three_genes(filter(pk_three_genes, scale == "raw count"), "Raw count") /
            (plot_three_genes(filter(pk_three_genes, scale == "log-CPM"), "log-CPM") + theme(strip.text = element_blank()))
    ) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
    ```

    At this point, we can, in principle, fit a linear model where the experimental
    factors are features $x_{n}$ and the transformed gene expression is teh response $y_n$.

20. But there are still issues. When we convert to frequencies, we're losing a
meaningful information about the precision of our measurements. Two samples can
have exactly the same logCPM value for a gene but different total counts.  The
total count information is important because a sample with deep sequencing is
measured more accurately than one with shallow sequencing.

21. This shows up in the spread of the groups after the logCPM transformation
has been applied. For example, in Figure 7^[From the airway dataset
above.], the logCPM transformation has put all the genes on roughly the same
scale. Instead of ranging from 0 to 40,000, they're in roughly the range from -5
to 10.

    ```{r}
    #| label: airway-treatment-setup
    #| echo: false
    #| include: false
    pal_dex <- c(trt = "#A53C61", untrt = "#487150")
    lab_dex <- c(untrt = "untreated", trt = "dexamethasone")
    airway_genes <- c("GAPDH", "DUSP1", "ZBTB16")

    airway_three_genes <- expression_scales(dge, airway_genes)

    # reused below for the YWHAB figure as well
    plot_by_treatment <- function(data, ylab, scales = "free_y") {
        ggplot(data, aes(dex, value)) +
            geom_line(aes(group = cell), colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.5) +
            geom_point(aes(size = lib.size / 1e6, colour = dex)) +
            scale_colour_manual(values = pal_dex, guide = "none") +
            scale_size(range = c(1.2, 5), name = "Library size (M reads)") +
            facet_wrap(~symbol, nrow = 1, scales = scales) +
            scale_x_discrete(labels = lab_dex, expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
            scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
            labs(x = NULL, y = ylab)
    }
    ```

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-airway-normalization-treatment
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 8
    #| fig-height: 4.6
    #| out-width: 650px
    (
        (plot_by_treatment(filter(airway_three_genes, scale == "raw count"), "Raw count") + labs(x = NULL)) /
            (plot_by_treatment(filter(airway_three_genes, scale == "log-CPM"), "log-CPM") + theme(strip.text = element_blank()))
    ) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")
    ```

    But notice that the ZBTB16 gene has more variation within each group
    compared to the other two genes. In statistical language, this is
    called the residual variation (after residualizing out the group effect),
    and it happens to be a general phenomenon that genes with smaller sequencing
    depth also have larger residual variation after the logCPM transformation.

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-airway-voom
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 6
    #| fig-height: 4.2
    #| out-width: 600px
    trend_points <- tibble(gene_id = rownames(v), mean_log_count = v$voom.xy$x, sqrt_sd = v$voom.xy$y) |>
        left_join(dge$genes, by = "gene_id")
    trend_line <- as_tibble(v$voom.line)

    ggplot(trend_points, aes(mean_log_count, sqrt_sd)) +
        geom_point(colour = ink[["muted"]], alpha = 0.15, size = 0.5) +
        geom_line(data = trend_line, aes(x, y), colour = pal_dex[["trt"]], linewidth = 1) +
        geom_point(data = filter(trend_points, symbol %in% airway_genes), colour = ink[["primary"]], size = 2) +
        geom_text_repel(data = filter(trend_points, symbol %in% airway_genes), aes(label = symbol), size = 3.2, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
        labs(x = expression("Average" ~ log[2] * "(count)"), y = "sqrt(residual SD)")
    ```

22. Limma uses this trend to reweight the observations. The curve above was
learned using gene-level quantities. But we can compute the quantity on the
x-axis for any count $y_{ng}$, and this suggests an associated weight, called
the precision weight. Intuitively, if an observation comes from a sample with
deep sequencing, it will have higher precision.

    These weights can then be incorporated into linear models through weighted
    linear regression. For example in the simple case where we're simply looking at
    the difference between two groups, we would compute a weighted average instead
    of a plain average.

## Multiple Hypothesis Testing

23. At this point, we could imagine applying a linear model to every single
genomic feature. We would have a separate null hypothesis associated with each
gene. We would reject those where the groups means seem different (controlling
for other factors). The resulting list of significant genes would be the ones
that we prioritize for follow-up analysis.

24. This doesn't quite work, though. It's easiest to understand through a small
example. I've simulated a thousand hypothetical genes from two groups. For
every gene, I simulated variances $\sigma_{g}^{2}$ from a uniform distribution
between 0.5 and 2, so some have expression that stay closer to their mean than
others. For 50 of these genes, I introduce a true difference of 2.5 between the
means^[The rest have means all equal to zero.]. In the language of the
two-groups model above, $\mu_{A} = 0, \mu_{B} = 2.5$. I sample only two
replicates per group (four samples total).

25. Figure 9a shows the 50 genes with the most significant $t$-statistics. Only
11 are actually related to the treatment! Of the top 10 genes, only two are
actually relevant.

    ```{r}
    #| label: many-genes-setup
    #| echo: false
    #| include: false
    n_genes_many <- 1000
    n_nonnull_many <- 50
    n_per_group2 <- 2
    effect2 <- 2.5

    gene_t_stats <- function(sim) {
        sim |>
            summarise(
                sigma = sigma[1],
                mean_A = mean(y[group == "A"]), mean_B = mean(y[group == "B"]),
                ss = sum((y[group == "A"] - mean_A)^2) + sum((y[group == "B"] - mean_B)^2),
                .by = gene
            ) |>
            mutate(
                df = 2 * n_per_group2 - 2,
                sd_hat = sqrt(ss / df),
                estimate = mean_A - mean_B,
                se = sd_hat * sqrt(2 / n_per_group2),
                t = estimate / se
            ) |>
            select(-ss)
    }

    sigma2_many <- runif(n_genes_many, 0.5, 2)
    many_genes <- expand_grid(gene = seq_len(n_genes_many), sample = seq_len(2 * n_per_group2)) |>
        mutate(
            group = if_else(sample <= n_per_group2, "A", "B"),
            mu = if_else(group == "A" & gene <= n_nonnull_many, effect2, 0),
            sigma = sqrt(sigma2_many[gene]),
            y = rnorm(n(), mu, sigma)
        ) |>
        gene_t_stats() |>
        mutate(
            truth = factor(if_else(gene <= n_nonnull_many, "truly non-null", "null"), levels = c("truly non-null", "null")),
            ratio = sd_hat / sigma,
            t_oracle = estimate / (sigma * sqrt(2 / n_per_group2)),
            rank = rank(-abs(t)),
            rank_oracle = rank(-abs(t_oracle))
        )

    # moderated t, in the style of limma::eBayes, for the last figure of this section
    shrunk_many <- limma::squeezeVar(many_genes$sd_hat^2, df = many_genes$df)
    many_genes <- many_genes |>
        mutate(
            sd_mod = sqrt(shrunk_many$var.post),
            se_mod = sd_mod * sqrt(2 / n_per_group2),
            t_moderated = estimate / se_mod,
            rank_moderated = rank(-abs(t_moderated))
        )

    pal_truth <- c("truly non-null" = "#4A7F94", "null" = "#d3c8a6")
    ```

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-top-genes
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 7
    #| fig-height: 6
    #| out-width: 600px
    top50 <- filter(many_genes, rank <= 50)
    top_t <- ggplot(top50, aes(rank, abs(t), colour = truth)) +
        geom_point(shape = 16, size = 2.2) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = pal_truth, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
        scale_y_log10() +
        labs(x = NULL, y = "|t| (log scale)")
    top_sd <- ggplot(top50, aes(rank, ratio, colour = truth)) +
        geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
        geom_point(shape = 16, size = 2.2) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = pal_truth, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
        expand_limits(y = 0) +
        labs(x = sprintf("Most significant |t|", nrow(many_genes)), y = "Estimated SD / true SD")
    (top_t / top_sd) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
    ```

    Figure 9b is the critical clue. The genes that appear most significant
    actually just have estimated variances $s_{g}^2$ that are smaller than their
    true variances $\sigma_{g}^2$, which we know in the simulation, but which we
    wouldn't know in reality. The problem is that with small sample sizes, we
    might have a small empirical variance just by chance, and since the
    $t$-statistic divides by $s_g$, we end up overestimating the associated
    genes' significance.

    $$
    t_{g} = \frac{\bar{y}_{A,g} - \bar{y}_{B,g}}{s_{g}\sqrt{1/N_A + 1/N_B}}.
    $$

26. When we observe a small $s_{g}^2$, it could either be because the gene truly
has small variation around its mean, or we just got replicates that are
unusually close to each other. The major insight of limma is that the other
genes can help us tell which of these two situations we are in.

    To this end, suppose we had a prior $H$ for the genewise variances,
    $$
    \sigma_{g}^{2} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} H
    $$
    This captures our prior knowledge about how much variation is expected
    in each group. Since the distribution of $s_{g}^2$ given $\sigma_{g}^{2}$
    has a known form, it is possible to compute a posterior for each gene $g$,
    $$
    p\left(\sigma_{g}^2 \vert s_{g}^2\right).
    $$
    This posterior gives a better estimate of $\sigma_{g}^2$ which we can use in
    place of $s_{g}^2$. Figure 10 shows the prior-to-posterior update for gene
    YWHAB, which had the smallest estimated $s_{g}^2$.

    ```{r}
    #| label: airway-shrinkage-setup
    #| echo: false
    #| include: false
    coef_dex <- "dextrt"
    q_airway <- 0.01

    # reused below for the Pickrell diagnostics as well
    shrinkage_table <- function(fit, coef, q = 0.01) {
        tibble(
            gene_id = rownames(fit),
            symbol = fit$genes$symbol,
            sd_raw = fit$sigma,
            sd_mod = sqrt(fit$s2.post),
            t_raw = fit$coefficients[, coef] / (fit$sigma * fit$stdev.unscaled[, coef]),
            t_mod = fit$t[, coef],
            p_mod = fit$p.value[, coef],
            adj_p = p.adjust(p_mod, method = "BH"),
            decision = factor(if_else(adj_p < q, "rejected", "not rejected"), levels = c("rejected", "not rejected"))
        )
    }
    pal_decision <- c("rejected" = "#2a78d6", "not rejected" = "#898781")
    plot_shrinkage <- function(data, q = 0.01) {
        ggplot(data, aes(t_raw, t_mod, colour = decision)) +
            geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["secondary"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
            geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.6) +
            scale_colour_manual(values = pal_decision, name = sprintf("BH at q = %s", q), drop = FALSE) +
            guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 2))) +
            coord_equal(xlim = c(-60, 60), ylim = c(-60, 60)) +
            labs(x = "Ordinary t-statistic", y = "Moderated t-statistic")
    }

    shrinkage <- shrinkage_table(fit, coef_dex, q_airway)

    # InvGamma prior/posterior density of a gene's underlying variance, on the log10 scale
    log_variance_density <- function(u, a, b) {
        precision <- 10^(-u)
        dgamma(precision, shape = a, rate = b) * precision * log(10)
    }

    variance_posterior_curve <- function(symbol_name) {
        row <- filter(shrinkage, symbol == symbol_name)
        df_prior <- fit$df.prior
        df_resid <- fit$df.residual[1]
        var_prior <- fit$s2.prior
        var_raw <- row$sd_raw^2
        var_mod <- row$sd_mod^2
        a_prior <- df_prior / 2
        b_prior <- df_prior * var_prior / 2
        a_post <- (df_prior + df_resid) / 2
        b_post <- (df_prior * var_prior + df_resid * var_raw) / 2
        lims <- range(
            1 / qgamma(c(0.001, 0.999), a_prior, rate = b_prior),
            1 / qgamma(c(0.001, 0.999), a_post, rate = b_post), var_raw, var_mod
        )
        grid <- seq(log10(lims[1]) - 0.08, log10(lims[2]) + 0.08, length.out = 1000)
        list(
            curves = bind_rows(
                tibble(log_variance = grid, density = log_variance_density(grid, a_prior, b_prior), distribution = "Fitted prior H"),
                tibble(log_variance = grid, density = log_variance_density(grid, a_post, b_post), distribution = "Posterior")
            ),
            markers = tibble(estimate = c("Initial estimate", "Moderated"), variance = c(var_raw, var_mod))
        )
    }
    ```

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-variance-posterior-low
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 4.5
    #| fig-height: 4.2
    #| out-width: 400px
    ywhab_post <- variance_posterior_curve("YWHAB")
    ggplot(ywhab_post$curves, aes(log_variance, density)) +
        geom_area(data = filter(ywhab_post$curves, distribution == "Posterior"), fill = "#3e6aa0", alpha = 0.12) +
        geom_line(aes(colour = distribution), linewidth = 0.9) +
        geom_vline(
            data = ywhab_post$markers, aes(xintercept = log10(variance), linetype = estimate),
            colour = ink[["primary"]], linewidth = 0.5
        ) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = c("Fitted prior H" = ink[["muted"]], "Posterior" = "#3e6aa0"), name = NULL) +
        scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Initial estimate" = "dashed", Moderated = "solid"), name = NULL) +
        scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01)(10^x)) +
        scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.06))) +
        labs(x = "Residual variance (log scale)", y = "Densities on log scale") +
        theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")
    ```

    How did limma choose the prior $H$? It turns out that it is possible to
    estimate $H$ by looking at the $s_{g}^2$ across all the genes. This is what
    is meant by limma performing empirical Bayes. Compared to standard Bayesian
    inference, where the prior must simply be assumed, we can use the many
    parallel genes to form an "empirical" prior $\hat{H}$, which can then flow
    into the posterior calculations.

27. A consequence of these updated $\sigma_{g}^2$ estimates is that the new,
"moderated" $t$-statistics are less affected by small values of $s_{g}^2$.
Looking across all genes, Figure 11 shows that the $t$-statistics are shrunken
towards zero. The genes that are shrunken the most are those whose $s_{g}^2$
were much lower than expected after estimating the prior variance $H$.

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-airway-shrinkage
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 6
    #| fig-height: 4.2
    #| out-width: 800px
    plot_shrinkage(shrinkage, q_airway)
    ```

    When using these $t$-statistics instead of the original ones, we have fewer
    false positives among our top-ranked genes. For example, returning to our
    earlier simulation, we can see that ranking using the moderated
    $t$-statistics leads to many fewer false positives and is nearly as good as
    using the ground truth standard deviation.

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-fraction-null-moderated
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 6.5
    #| fig-height: 3.6
    #| out-width: 550px
    fraction_null_top_k <- function(results, rank_col, k_max) {
        results |>
            arrange(.data[[rank_col]]) |>
            slice_head(n = k_max) |>
            transmute(k = row_number(), fraction_null = cummean(truth == "null"))
    }

    pal_ranking <- c("ordinary t" = "#0b0b0b", "t with the true SD" = "#898781", "moderated t" = "#4a3aa7")
    curves <- bind_rows(
        `ordinary t` = fraction_null_top_k(many_genes, "rank", 100),
        `t with the true SD` = fraction_null_top_k(many_genes, "rank_oracle", 100),
        `moderated t` = fraction_null_top_k(many_genes, "rank_moderated", 100),
        .id = "statistic"
    )
    ggplot(curves, aes(k, fraction_null, colour = statistic)) +
        geom_step(linewidth = 0.7) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = pal_ranking, name = "Ranked by", breaks = names(pal_ranking)) +
        scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::label_percent()) +
        labs(x = "k", y = "Null genes among the top k")
    ```

28. There's one last statistical consideration. If we use the usual hypothesis
testing cutoffs then we're liable to return many false positives...

    <img src="figures/significant.png" width=400/>

    The problem is that the hypothesis testing cutoffs were originally designed
    so that, under the null hypothesis, the probability of a false positive is
    $\alpha$ (usually 0.05). But as we test more and more hypotheses, the
    probability of encountering at least one false positive grows.

29. To deal with this phenomenon [@Benjamini1995] had the idea that instead of
controlling the probability of a single false positive, we should control the
proportion of false positives among all rejections. Formally, let $H_{1}, \dots,
H_{G}$ represent the null hypothesis for the $G$ genes.  Suppose we obtain
p-values $p_{1}, \dots, p_{G}$ and that $R$ of these $p$-values are smaller than
$\alpha$. The $R$ rejections are the discoveries we would comment on in our
paper. Among them, suppose that $V$ are false discoveries (in practice, we would
never know this).  The quantity

    $$
    \widehat{\mathrm{FDP}} = \frac{V}{R\vee 1}
    $$
    is the empirical false discovery proportion in this one experiment and its
    expected value across many experiments with the same underlying distribution
    is called the false discovery rate,
    $$
    \mathrm{FDR} = \mathbb{E}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{FDP}}\right]
    $$

30. In addition to introducing this quantity, Benjamini and Hochberg proposed a
way of adjusting the $p$-value cutoffs $\alpha_{k}$ so that if we reject
hypotheses using these cutoffs instead of $\alpha$, we would provably control
the false discovery rate. Their procedure is now called the Benjamini-Hochberg
(or BH) procedure, and the thresholds $\alpha_{k}$ are plotted as the magenta
line in panel (B) below.

    * Sort the $G$ p-values in increasing order,
     $$
     p_{(1)} \le p_{(2)} \le \cdots \le p_{(G)}
     $$
     and denote the associated nulls by $H_{(1)}, \dots, H_{(G)}$.
    * Fix an FDR target $q$^[This is the analog of $\alpha$ in ordinary hypothesis testing] and define new thresholds $\alpha_{k} = \frac{kq}{G}$. This means that the smallest p-value is compared to the strictest threshold, the next smallest is compared to a slightly more lenient one, etc.
    * Find the largest $k$ where $p_{(k)} \le \alpha_{k}$, and reject $H_{(1)}, \dots, H_{(k)}$. If there is no such $k$, don't reject anything.

    ```{r}
    #| label: bh_summary
    #| echo: false
    q <- 0.01
    pal_decision <- c("rejected" = "#2a78d6", "not rejected" = "#898781")
    scale_decision <- function(q) scale_colour_manual(values = pal_decision, name = sprintf("BH at q = %s", q), drop = FALSE)

    J  <- nrow(shrinkage)
    bh <- shrinkage |>
      arrange(p_mod) |>
      mutate(k = row_number(), threshold = k * q / J, under = p_mod <= threshold)
    k_max <- max(bh$k[bh$under])

    p_hist <- ggplot(shrinkage, aes(p_mod)) +
      geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.025), fill = ink[["muted"]], colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = J * 0.025, colour = pal_dex[["trt"]], linewidth = 0.6) +
      annotate("text", x = 1, y = J * 0.025, label = "all null", hjust = 1, vjust = -0.5, size = 3.2, colour = pal_dex[["trt"]]) +
      labs(x = "p-value", y = "Number of genes")

    p_stairs <- ggplot(filter(bh, k <= 1.5 * k_max), aes(k, p_mod)) +
      geom_line(aes(y = threshold), colour = pal_dex[["trt"]], linewidth = 0.6) +
      geom_point(aes(colour = decision), size = 0.6) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = k_max, linetype = "dotted", colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
      scale_decision(q) +
      guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2))) +
      scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
      labs(x = "Rank k of the p-value", y = expression(p[(k)]))

    p_bh <- (p_hist | p_stairs) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
    p_bh
    ```

31. This procedure can be justified through the histogram of $p$-values, like
those in panel (A) above. These $p$-values can be intuitively understood as a
mixture of those from significant genes (large peak with small $p$-values) and
those from nulls (everything else). Let $\pi_{0}$ denote the histogram density
after the peak levels off. When many of the hypotheses are null, then the peak
would be smaller and $\pi_{0}$ would be larger^[In fact, $\pi_{0}$ exactly
corresponds to the proportion of null hypothesis. The horizontal pink line in
panel (A) is the case that all genes are null and $\pi_{0} = 1$.].

    <img src="figures/mixture representation.png" width=400/>

    Normalize the histogram to have the total area of 1, so each gene has weight
    $\frac{1}{G}$. If we let $R\left(t\right)$ give the total number of rejections
    below a threshold $t$, the corresponding area to the left of this histogram is
    $\frac{R\left(t\right)}{G}$.

    <img src="figures/rejection density.png" width=400/>

    How much of this area do we think comes from the null hypotheses? A reasonable
    estimate is $\pi_{0}t$.

    <img src="figures/null rejection region.png" width=400/>

    So, a good estimate of the false discovery rate is the second area divided
    by the first,

    $$
    \mathrm{FDR}\left(t\right) \approx \frac{G\pi_{0}t}{R\left(t\right)}.
    $$

32. How might we choose $t$ so that the FDR is controlled below a target level
$q$? Suppose we set $t$ to the $k^{th}$ largest $p$-value, $p_{\left(k\right)}$.
Then we would have $k$ rejections, i.e. $R\left(t\right) = k$. Substituting this
into $t$ and $R\left(t\right)$, we find,

    $$
    \begin{align}
    \mathrm{FDR}\left(t\right) \leq q
    \iff \frac{G \pi_{0} p_{\left(k\right)}}{k} \leq q
    \iff p_{\left(k\right)} \leq \frac{kq}{G \pi_{0}}.
    \end{align}
    $$

    Approximating^[In fact, $\pi_{0}$ is always less than 1, so replacing it
    with one only makes our FDR estimate more conservative.] $\pi_{0} \approx 1$
    (i.e., most genes are null), the right hand side is $\alpha_{k}$. So, if we
    want to reject as many hypothesis as possible while controlling the FDR
    below $q$, then we should choose the largest $p_{\left(k\right)} \leq
    \alpha_{k}$. This is exactly the BH procedure.

33. This isn't exactly a proof, but hopefully it gives some intuition about
where the BH procedure came from. Finally, while it's nice to know where the
multiple testing correction comes from, we never have to compute the
Benjamini-Hochberg thresholds ourselves. When we run `topTable`, limma
automatically performs this multiple testing correction.

## Extra Code Example

34. Next we'll study data from Pickrell et al. (2010), who gathered RNA-seq data
from lymphoblastoid cell lines across 69 HapMap donors. Later research has
focused on sex differences in gene expression, which we'll analyze here.
Compared to the motivating airway example, the sample size is much larger. This
makes the moderated $t$-statistics less essential, as we will see.

    ```{r}
    library(tweeDEseqCountData)
    data(pickrell1)

    counts <- exprs(pickrell1.eset)
    samples <- data.frame(sex = factor(pickrell1.eset$gender), row.names = colnames(counts))
    genes <- data.frame(gene_id = rownames(counts), row.names = rownames(counts))
    dge <- DGEList(counts = counts, samples = samples, genes = genes)
    dge
    ```

35. As before, the first step is to filter genes that have low expression. This
reduces the data from 38410 to 18189 rows (we have so many genes because RNA-seq
picks up on the noncoding RNAs).

    ```{r}
    keep <- filterByExpr(dge, group = dge$samples$sex)
    dge <- normLibSizes(dge[keep, ])
    ```

36. Next we apply the logCPM normalization and recover expression weights. This
depends on the `design` because the residual variances are computed after the
initial regression onto `sex`.

    ```{r}
    design <- model.matrix(~sex, data = dge$samples)
    v <- voom(dge, design)
    ```

37. The weights and original design are passed to the linear model, and the
variances are shrunk towards the prior mean in the empirical Bayes step.

    ```{r}
    fit_raw <- lmFit(v, design)
    fit <- eBayes(fit_raw)
    ```

    Plotting the original vs. moderated $t$-statistics shows that, with more
    samples, the empirical bayes shrinkage step has less effect than it did in the
    airway dataset.

    ```{r}
    #| label: fig-pickrell-shrinkage
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-width: 6
    #| fig-height: 4.2
    #| out-width: 800px
    coef_sex <- "sexmale"
    q_pickrell <- 0.01

    shrinkage_pickrell <- shrinkage_table(fit, coef_sex, q_pickrell)
    plot_shrinkage(shrinkage_pickrell, q_pickrell)
    ```

38. Looking
up^[The source data uses the hg19 reference genome, which is why the ENSEMBL IDs
look different.] the most significant genes, we see that the
[first](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/140032) and
[third](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/246126) are Y-linked and the
[second](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/7503?utm_source=gemini) is associated
with X inactivation.

    ```{r}
    topTable(fit, coef = "sexmale")
    ```

## Learning More

39. All the figures in this notebook are created using code that's directly
executed inline. All the statistical quantities, like the moderated t-statistics
and the prior and posterior variances, were extracted from limma. You can rerun
our [source code](https://github.com/krisrs1128/talks/blob/master/2026/20260923/20260923.qmd)
to get hands-on experience, and I encourage you to try making these kinds of
plots on your own data.

40. You can find many more code examples in the Limma [online manual](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/limma/inst/doc/usersguide.pdf).

41. Limma is just one strategy for multiple testing with RNA-seq data. Another
Bioconductor-based approach is DESeq2 [@love2014moderated]. It applies
generalized linear models rather than linear models, which is a bit more
conceptually advanced. But the software is also well developed and the key
concepts like normalization, empirical Bayesian shrinkage, and multiple testing
all carry over.

42. The simulation in the multiple testing section was inspired by a similar one
in [@ji2010analyzing]. It also motivates a Bayesian approach to sharing
information across genes.  A deep Empirical Bayesian analysis of the limma is
given by [@Ignatiadis2025]. What the original limma paper presents as a somewhat
ad hoc recipe this paper shows is an immediate consequence of some basic (and
reasonable) statistical assumptions.

43. [Chapter 6](https://web.stanford.edu/class/bios221/book/06-chap.html#multiple-testing) of
[@Holmes2019-bl] gives a great introduction to multiple testing in
high-throughput omics, and it's available for free online.
